narrative:
The hearing was meant to end with Mara’s rival, Iven, named as the saboteur. The ledger lay open beneath the magistrate’s hand, its missing page enough to make the accusation convenient and its remaining figures enough to make it plausible. Mara had spent the night finding the flaw in the case. She had also spent it deciding how much of the truth she could afford to save.

When the magistrate called for testimony, Mara did not deny that Iven had entered the archive. She denied the more useful detail: that he had been alone. The room tightened around the omission. Iven turned toward her, suspicion sharper than gratitude. He knew she would not spend a kindness without charging for it.

“I can identify the person who removed the page,” Mara said, “but only if the hearing is closed and Iven’s seal is restored first.”

The magistrate threatened her with contempt. Mara’s fingers closed around the evidence box, though her voice stayed dry. “Then you may have a public answer, and an incorrect one. I’m sure the archive will treasure the distinction.”

Iven resisted before the magistrate could respond. He accused her of arranging a bargain to save herself, and for one moment Mara nearly let him. A confession would have been simpler than watching him mistake protection for manipulation. Instead, she offered the box across the table.

“Your seal,” she said. “My name removed from the report. After that, you hear what I know.”

He studied her—not trusting her, but recognizing the cost. If he accepted, he surrendered the chance to expose her involvement. If he refused, the magistrate would take the accusation as settled. His hand hovered over the box. Mara did not urge him. Fear showed only in the choice she would not make for him.

Iven accepted. The magistrate, irritated by the loss of an easy verdict, ordered the room cleared. Before the doors shut, Iven leaned close.

“One day,” he murmured, “you’ll explain why you keep rescuing people you despise.”

“Don’t be ambitious,” Mara said. “I’m only preserving the value of having an enemy.”

The bargain protected him and bound him to her account, but it did not make them allies. Outside the hearing room, he returned her evidence box without thanks. Mara took it without apology. The apology had already been made—in the price she demanded, and in the fact that she had paid one herself.
title: The Price of Standing Aside
